overview: Wise is a global fintech building infrastructure for cross-border money movement and international financial accounts, serving personal and business customers directly as well as banks and enterprises via its Wise Platform API. Originally UK-founded (as TransferWise, 2011), the group reorganized in May 2026 under a new Jersey holding company (Wise Group plc) and moved its primary stock listing to Nasdaq (WSE) while retaining a secondary London listing (WISE, quoted in GBp), switching its reporting currency from GBP to USD starting with FY2026 results. In FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026) Wise generated $2,502.8m of net revenue (+19% YoY), $498.7m of net income and $660.4m of income before tax across 18.9m active customers in the year (+21%) moving $243.5bn cross-border (+31%, take rate down to 0.52% from 0.58% in FY2025 and 0.67% in FY2024), with customer holdings up 40% to $39.0bn; Q1 FY2027 (quarter ended 30 June 2026) extended that momentum (net revenue $714.0m, volume $69.3bn +26%, holdings $41.2bn +31%, take rate 0.50%). But the business continues to work through a cluster of serious AML/compliance-related regulatory and legal setbacks: a Belgian criminal money-laundering investigation into Wise Europe SA disclosed in June 2026 (stock -16-20% over the following days) that led to a public National Bank of Belgium remedial order in August 2026 (a reputational, no-fine supervisory measure requiring full AML/CTF compliance by 31 January 2027, with the separate Brussels criminal prosecution still unresolved), a US multi-state Consent Order (July 2025, $4.2m fine), the OCC's outright denial of Wise's US national trust bank charter application (21-24 July 2026), and now US securities class actions filed in September 2026 (Kaplan Fox, Faruqi, Glancy, Levi & Korsinsky; class period 11 May-23 July 2026, lead-plaintiff deadline 29 September 2026) alleging Wise understated these AML/CTF risks to investors around the Nasdaq listing. Against that backdrop, Wise's 24 September 2026 AGM passed all resolutions (including buyback authority) with ~99.98% support, and the company has continued steadily executing its up-to-£405m Goldman Sachs-run buyback — together raising real questions about the durability of Wise's 'regulated, low-cost rail' moat versus its historical framing as a clean, compliance-light challenger to banks, even as the underlying growth and cash generation remain strong.

business_model.summary: Wise earns money primarily from small percentage fees on cross-border transfers and currency conversion (transaction revenue), supplemented by card usage/subscription fees and by interest earned on customer balances held on the platform (net of interest paid out to customers). The model is built around continuously lowering the effective price (take rate) to drive volume, referral-based growth, and cross-sell of account features, which in turn increases customer balances and non-transfer revenue. Non-cross-border activities (cards, account features, interest) now represent just over half of total net revenue, evidencing the diversification strategy.

revenue_streams.name: Cross-border transfer revenue
revenue_streams.description: Fees on international money transfers; FY2026 cross-border take rate fell to 0.52% (from 0.58% in FY2025 and 0.67% in FY2024) and Q1 FY27 take rate was 0.50%, as the company continues deliberate price reduction, with management/press coverage indicating a target of ~46bps by FY27 to defend cost leadership against stablecoin competition

revenue_streams.name: Card and other transaction revenue
revenue_streams.description: Debit card interchange/usage and other account-based fees; grew 38% YoY to $191.1m in Q1 FY27, the fastest-growing revenue line

revenue_streams.name: Interest income on customer balances (net)
revenue_streams.trend: growing with balances, sensitive to rates
revenue_streams.description: Interest earned on customer float ($806.1m gross interest income in FY2026, offset by $196.9m interest paid to customers = ~$609m net); in Q1 FY27 gross interest income was $225.4m (+15% YoY) against $52.3m interest expense; grows with customer holdings but is a headwind when central banks cut rates

business_model.customer_type: B2C (personal customers, ~11.3m of the ~11.9m active customer base), B2B (Wise Business, ~608k business customers, +28% YoY), and B2B2C (Wise Platform — banks and enterprises embedding Wise infrastructure, e.g., Standard Chartered, Morgan Stanley, Nubank, UniCredit)
business_model.geographic_mix: Global operations across 40+ countries with licenses in 80+ markets (48 US states plus four territories); core revenue concentrated in UK/Europe (~27% of group net revenue, including the entity now under Belgian criminal investigation and a National Bank of Belgium remedial order, Wise Europe SA), North America, and Australia, with expanding presence in Brazil, Japan, UAE, Singapore and Latin America (recently expanded product in Chile)
business_model.unit_economics: Take rate has fallen from ~0.67% in FY2024 to 0.52% in FY2026 and 0.50% in Q1 FY27 as management deliberately reinvests scale efficiencies into price cuts, betting that volume growth and word-of-mouth referral (majority of new customers) more than offset the lower unit fee. Customer holdings ($41.2bn as of Q1 FY27, +31% YoY; $39.0bn at FY2026 year-end, +40% YoY) are growing faster than transfer volumes, diversifying revenue away from pure transaction fees.

main_competitors: emerging stablecoin-based payment rails (Tether/Anchorage's USAT, Bridge/USDC-integrated challengers)
competitive_position.market_position: Leading independent cross-border payments specialist by volume and brand recognition among digitally-native transfer providers; still a low single-digit percentage share of the multi-trillion-dollar global cross-border payments market (personal + SMB + enterprise), implying a long runway if it can continue taking share from banks, which still handle the bulk of global cross-border flows at much higher cost — though 2026's string of AML enforcement actions and now securities litigation has dented the narrative that Wise's compliance program is inherently superior to incumbent banks'.
competitive_position.market_share: Low single digits of total addressable cross-border flows; roughly mid-single-digit share of the addressable personal remittance/transfer market and a much smaller share of the SMB/enterprise segment, where Wise Platform is still nascent

moat_factors.description: Over a decade of direct integrations into domestic payment systems (e.g., Pix in Brazil, Zengin in Japan, faster payments in UK, ACH in US, InstaPay) allows Wise to avoid correspondent banking chains, delivering 77% of transfers instantly (Q1 FY27, up from 70% a year earlier) at a structural cost advantage that is very difficult and slow for competitors to replicate

moat_factors.strength: strong on breadth, credibility now impaired
moat_factors.description: 80+ licenses across jurisdictions (including 48 US states and four territories as a money transmitter) create both a barrier to entry for new competitors and the foundation for Wise Platform's B2B2C model; however, the July 2026 OCC denial of Wise's US national trust bank charter, the August 2026 National Bank of Belgium public remedial order against Wise Europe SA (customer due-diligence and transaction-monitoring deficiencies, compliance required by 31 January 2027), the still-unresolved Brussels criminal AML investigation, and the 2025 US multi-state Consent Order together mean the license footprint is now accompanied by a real, recent, multi-jurisdictional track record of AML/CFT enforcement findings rather than a clean regulatory record — a meaningful dent to a moat argument built partly on 'we are the compliant alternative to informal/unregulated rails'

Scale plus direct rail access lets Wise offer an average fee of ~50bps versus wide bank FX spreads (often 2-5%+), and each incremental volume unit lowers unit servicing cost, funding further price cuts — a virtuous cycle competitors without comparable infrastructure struggle to match profitably

As more banks and fintechs (Standard Chartered, Morgan Stanley, Nubank, UniCredit, Monzo, Ramp, Brex) embed Wise's infrastructure, the volume flowing through Wise's rails increases, improving liquidity, pricing, and further justifying rail investment — a classic infrastructure network effect still in early innings (Platform volume share modest but rising)

Reputation for transparent, low-cost pricing has historically driven a large share of new customer acquisition organically, lowering customer acquisition cost versus better-funded, marketing-heavy rivals like Revolut; the Belgium probe/NBB order, the OCC denial, and the newly filed US securities class actions are the first meaningful, compounding dents to a brand built substantially on trust and regulatory cleanliness

$41.2bn of customer holdings (Q1 FY27, +31% YoY) sitting in Wise accounts (including Wise Assets investment products, now $10.2bn AUC, +55% YoY) create stickiness akin to a banking relationship, beyond a one-off transfer transaction

weaknesses: Brand awareness still trails PayPal and Revolut in several core markets, requiring sustained (and now tripled) marketing investment
Take-rate compression is structural to the strategy, meaning Wise must continually grow volumes faster than price declines to grow revenue — a treadmill dynamic
Wise Platform (bank/enterprise B2B2C channel) remains a small proportion of total volume despite years of investment and marquee partnerships — the RFP-driven sales cycle with large banks is slow
Reliance on interest income (still ~24% of net revenue) introduces earnings volatility tied to central bank policy outside management's control

AML/CFT execution gap now documented across three separate jurisdictions within roughly a year: the July 2025 US multi-state Consent Order, the OCC's July 2026 charter-denial letter describing 'continuing noncompliance' and a 'persistent inability to sufficiently manage' ML/TF risk, and the National Bank of Belgium's August 2026 public remedial order against Wise Europe SA over customer due-diligence, intra-group information-sharing and transaction-monitoring deficiencies (compliance required by 31 January 2027) — a pattern that reads as systemic (same root-cause finding of inadequate client/activity identification recurring across entities) rather than a single one-off lapse

Belgium remains the more structurally dangerous of the 2026 regulatory events even after the August 2026 NBB order: that order was a reputational, no-fine supervisory measure (Belgium's new AML 'name-and-shame' regime), but the separate Brussels Public Prosecutor's criminal investigation into Wise Europe SA over EUR500m+ of suspicious flows tied to fraud, corruption and drug trafficking across hundreds of criminal files from 30+ countries remains unresolved as of early October 2026, with prosecutors reported since June 2026 to be finalizing a direct criminal-court summons (bypassing an investigating judge) — a licence-level tail risk for the EU entity that generates roughly a quarter of group net revenue

US regulatory credibility gap versus fintech peers: independent commentary notes 8 of 11 resolved OCC national-trust-charter applications from fintechs since 2020 were approved outright, making Wise's outright denial the outlier rather than the industry norm — undercutting the 'the whole industry got caught by a Fed policy shift' framing Wise has used publicly; the OCC's own letter explicitly states enforcement actions 'do not ultimately control' its charter decisions, i.e., it treats the underlying AML deficiencies, not merely the Consent Order's existence, as decisive

New US securities litigation overhang: multiple firms (Kaplan Fox, Faruqi, Glancy, Levi & Korsinsky) filed/announced class actions in September 2026 on behalf of purchasers of WSE/WISE securities between 11 May 2026 and 23 July 2026, alleging Wise made materially false or misleading statements about its AML/CFT controls and US charter prospects around the Nasdaq listing; lead-plaintiff deadline was 29 September 2026, with no damages figure, settlement, or motion-to-dismiss outcome yet disclosed

Stablecoin strategy is still at a 'refile a charter application' stage rather than a launched product, and Wise's plan to pursue a GENIUS Act-aligned charter has no confirmed submission date or approval certainty, leaving Wise reactive versus faster-moving stablecoin infrastructure already live in the market (e.g., Tether/Anchorage's USAT)

growth_drivers: Wise Platform scaling: embedding Wise infrastructure inside banks and fintechs (Standard Chartered's SC Remit, Morgan Stanley corporate cross-border settlement, Nubank, UniCredit, Itau, Monzo, Ramp, Brex) to access those institutions' large existing customer bases

Continued direct payment-rail build-out (Pix in Brazil, Zengin in Japan, and further domestic system integrations) driving faster settlement (77% instant in Q1 FY27, up from 70% a year earlier) and lower unit costs that can be reinvested in price

Account/holdings deepening: Wise Assets and multi-currency account balances ($41.2bn in Q1 FY27, +31% YoY; $39.0bn at FY2026 year-end, +40% YoY) diversify revenue beyond transactional fees and increase customer lifetime value; Assets under custody alone grew 55% YoY to $10.2bn
Geographic expansion into underpenetrated corridors: UAE, Brazil, South Africa, Japan, and Latin America (e.g., recent Chile product expansion enabling local instant pay-ins)
Business/SMB segment growth (608k business customers, +28% YoY; business volume +39% YoY) as cross-border commerce and remote/globalized work increase demand for multi-currency accounts

Emerging adjacent revenue lines beyond the core transfer/interest/card model: card acceptance, investment/Wise Assets products, subscription-style collection tools, and early-stage stablecoin/digital-asset interoperability features, per external job-posting and product analysis, offer some diversification independent of the US charter's fate

Nasdaq primary listing intended to raise US profile, broaden the investor base, and support the long-term ambition to capture more of the multi-trillion-dollar cross-border payments market, potentially aiding further US bank/enterprise partnerships

Planned refiled US national trust bank charter application under a GENIUS Act stablecoin/payments framework: management has signaled it will resubmit given the evolving US regulatory landscape (GENIUS Act, shifting Fed master-account policy), which if eventually approved could still deliver direct Fed payment-system access and materially lower US operating costs, though timing remains unconfirmed as of October 2026 and approval is far from assured given the OCC's explicit AML-adequacy objections

Secular tailwinds: continued digitization of payments, G20-driven push for cheaper/faster cross-border retail payments, and growing global mobility/remote work increasing personal and business cross-border money movement

Optionality on digital-asset/stablecoin infrastructure: management describes Wise's rail network as 'extendable' to incorporate stablecoins for money movement, has explicitly linked its next US charter application to a GENIUS Act framework, and press coverage indicates a target of accelerating price cuts toward a ~46bps take rate by FY27 to defend cost leadership specifically against stablecoin competition, preserving a call option on this emerging technology rather than ceding it entirely to challengers

regulatory.risk: US national trust bank charter denial
regulatory.description: On 21 July 2026 (communicated 23-24 July) the OCC formally denied Wise's application (filed June 2025) for a national trust bank charter (Wise National Trust, Austin TX; Corporate Decision #1381, Control Number 2025-Charter-342106), citing inability to conclude Wise would run an effective AML/CFT program, organizers/management with insufficient AML/CFT and fiduciary experience, and Wise US's 'continuing noncompliance' referencing the July 2025 multi-state Consent Order. The letter states the OCC 'cannot conclude the proposed national trust bank will have an effective AML/CFT compliance program... until Wise has addressed existing deficiencies,' and that proposed management and the board 'demonstrated a persistent inability to sufficiently manage the ML/TF AML/CFT risks.' Wise has said it will refile under a GENIUS Act framework; no confirmed submission date as of October 2026, and the Consent Order's independent-validation/SAR-lookback requirements (through July 2027) likely gate any credible refiling. WSE/WISE shares fell ~6-11% on the news (24 July 2026)

regulatory.risk: Belgian AML investigation and National Bank of Belgium remedial order (Wise Europe SA)
regulatory.description: Disclosed publicly in June 2026, Belgian prosecutors have been investigating Wise Europe SA since 2025 over indications of AML noncompliance — particularly inadequate client/activity identification — tied to more than EUR500m in suspicious transactions drawn from hundreds of criminal files (fraud, corruption, drug trafficking) referred via European Investigation Orders and international letters rogatory from 30+ countries. On 25 August 2026 the National Bank of Belgium (Wise's EU prudential/passporting supervisor) publicly issued a remedial order against Wise Europe SA — the first company named under Belgium's new AML 'name-and-shame' disclosure policy — citing serious customer-due-diligence, intra-group information-sharing, ongoing-monitoring and unusual-activity-detection deficiencies, and requiring full compliance by 31 January 2027; notably this order imposed no fine (a reputational, not monetary, sanction). Separately, and still unresolved as of early October 2026, the Brussels Public Prosecutor's Office's criminal investigation continues, with prosecutors reported (since June 2026) to be finalizing a direct summons to take the case straight to criminal court (bypassing an investigating judge). Because Wise Europe SA underpins the EU passporting licenses supporting roughly 27% of group net revenue, an adverse criminal finding remains a licence-level tail risk materially larger in potential severity than the resolved NBB administrative matter, even though the administrative order itself proved less punitive (no fine) than initially feared; shares fell as much as ~16-20% over 1-3 June 2026 when the investigation was first reported.

Operating under 80+ licenses globally requires continuous investment (roughly a third of headcount touches compliance/financial crime); the July 2025 multi-state Consent Order (Order No. 2025-013; California, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas, Massachusetts, plus a separate California DFPI order; $4.2m fine split among regulators) followed a 2024 multi-state examination (covering Jul-2022 to Sep-2023) and cited suspicious-activity investigation/reporting failures, transaction-monitoring data-integrity gaps, untimely SAR filings, failure to independently review the AML program at an adequate frequency, failure to timely remediate prior examination findings, and Remittance Transfer Rule violations. It mandates a lookback review of accounts closed March 2023-March 2025, enhanced monitoring/SAR procedures, and ongoing regulator reporting, with obligations continuing through July 2027 — a tail that both delays any credible US charter refiling and keeps Wise under active multi-state supervision through at least mid-2027; no update to its terms has been reported since it took effect

Beginning September 2026, multiple plaintiffs' firms (Kaplan Fox, Faruqi, Glancy, Levi & Korsinsky) announced/filed federal securities class actions on behalf of purchasers of Wise Group plc (WSE/WISE) securities during the class period 11 May 2026-23 July 2026, alleging the company made materially false or misleading statements regarding its AML/CTF controls and the regulatory risk facing its pending US trust bank charter application, which were then revealed via the 1 June 2026 Belgian AML probe disclosure and the 23-24 July 2026 OCC charter denial. Lead-plaintiff deadline was 29 September 2026; no complaint consolidation, motion-to-dismiss ruling, damages estimate, or settlement has been disclosed as of early October 2026. WSE shares fell a cumulative 16.05% over 1-3 June 2026 and a further ~6.2% on 24 July 2026, the price declines plaintiffs' counsel are using as the basis for alleged investor losses; no reserve or contingent-liability provision has been disclosed by Wise to date.

The 2025 shareholder vote extended CEO Kristo Käärmann's Class B supervoting shares (originally due to sunset in 2026) by another decade (to 2036) alongside the US listing move; co-founder Taavet Hinrikus publicly opposed the extension, and the concentrated ~50% voting control despite ~18% economic interest is a recurring governance overhang cited by some investors and proxy advisors, and arguably relevant to the OCC's stated concerns about organizers/management/board depth, experience, and accountability. The 24 September 2026 AGM nonetheless passed all eight resolutions (financial statements, auditor matters, four director elections, and share buyback authorization) by strong majorities, with the buyback resolution drawing 99.98% support (2,097,582,802 votes for vs. 343,312 against; ~74.89% of issued share capital voted)

Evolving AML/data protection/payment-system regulation (EU DORA, expanding FinCEN/BSA requirements, the US GENIUS Act's new stablecoin framework, and evolving Federal Reserve master-account access policy) increases compliance costs and creates near-term uncertainty (as evidenced by the OCC denial and the Belgian probe/NBB order) but could also benefit Wise's transparent-pricing/regulated model over less-regulated alternatives long-term if it can clear the bar

business.description: Revolut, Remitly, Airwallex, Nium, and traditional banks (which are improving digital/cross-border offerings) all compete on price and speed; continued commoditization pressures take rates further

GENIUS Act-aligned stablecoin infrastructure is now live in the US market (e.g., Tether/Anchorage's USAT, issued via an OCC-chartered bank structure with US Treasury/FDIC-backed reserves), and Remitly has integrated Bridge's stablecoin infrastructure into treasury/settlement operations. Wise's own strategy has shifted from a passive 'monitor and stay extendable' posture toward an active (but as-yet unfiled) plan to refile for a US trust bank charter under a GENIUS Act framework, and toward accelerated price cuts (press reports cite a ~46bps take-rate target by FY27) to defend cost leadership, meaning Wise is now racing to catch up on regulated stablecoin rails rather than leading, with approval timing uncertain after its first application was denied

Bank/enterprise partnerships take years to scale from signing to material volume; large partners could also build competing in-house capability or select alternative providers via competitive RFPs; unverified market chatter has also questioned the depth of some flagship partnerships
Revenue growth depends on volume growth outpacing continued fee compression; a slowdown in customer/volume growth without an offsetting take-rate stabilization would directly hit revenue growth

financial.description: $806.1m of FY2026 net revenue came from gross interest income on customer balances (~24% of net revenue net of interest paid), with FY2026 retained-float yield of ~2.22% versus a more normalized long-run assumption closer to ~1.5%; global central bank rate cuts (already underway in several markets) are a direct headwind to this revenue line even as balances grow; FY2027 guidance explicitly assumes no material change in central bank policy rates from current levels

Revenue and costs span many currencies; the switch to USD reporting increases visibility of FX translation effects on reported growth versus constant-currency growth (Q1 FY27 cross-border volume grew 26% reported vs. 24% constant-currency)

$41.2bn+ of customer holdings creates quasi-banking risk; funds are held in safeguarded accounts/government securities but scale itself increases scrutiny and operational risk, underscored by both the OCC's characterization of Wise's US AML/CFT program as not commensurate with its enterprise-wide volume/risk, and the National Bank of Belgium's finding that Wise Europe SA's customer due-diligence and monitoring controls fell short

FY2026 operating income fell to $590.7m from $728.2m in FY2025 despite revenue growth, reflecting a deliberate step-up in technology, servicing, marketing, and G&A spend (compliance/servicing opex now looks like a structural, permanent reset near 30-31% of net revenue rather than a temporary spike, meaning the pre-2025 34-37% income-before-tax margin era is unlikely to return); FY2026 income-before-tax margin still came in ahead of guidance, and the up-to-£405m/$540m buyback (launched 21 July 2026) is progressing steadily (e.g., ~1.49m shares repurchased across Nasdaq/LSE in the week of 21-25 September 2026 alone) signaling continued confidence in free cash flow generation despite the litigation/regulatory overhang

macro.description: As major central banks (Fed, BoE, ECB) continue cutting rates through 2026-2027, net interest income on the ~$41bn+ customer balance book will likely decline as a percentage yield (FY2026 retained float yield ~2.22% vs. a more normalized ~1.5% assumption), partially offset by balance growth

Cross-border transfer volumes (personal remittances and SMB trade payments) are correlated with global trade activity, migration patterns, and consumer/business confidence; a recession would likely slow volume growth
Operating across 40+ countries exposes Wise to sanctions regimes, capital controls, and political instability that can disrupt specific payment corridors

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global cross-border payments market (personal, SMB, and enterprise combined) is estimated in the tens of trillions of dollars annually and continues to grow, with structural share shift underway from expensive correspondent-banking/bank-FX-spread models toward transparent digital challengers and real-time payment rails. Stablecoins are an emerging disruptive force, increasingly formalized in the US by the GENIUS Act and already live via products like Tether/Anchorage's USAT; Wise has moved from a passive monitoring posture to actively planning a GENIUS Act-aligned charter refile and accelerated price cuts, but its first charter attempt was denied by the OCC in July 2026 on AML-adequacy grounds, and — set against the Belgian criminal AML probe, the August 2026 National Bank of Belgium remedial order against its EU entity, and the September 2026 US securities class actions — 2026 has become a year in which Wise's regulatory/compliance and legal standing, not its product or distribution, is the central investment debate, even as underlying operating momentum (volume, revenue, customer growth, buyback execution) remains robust.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — cross-border volumes correlate with global trade, migration, and business activity, but personal remittances have historically been relatively resilient through downturns; Wise Platform (B2B2C) partnerships offer some diversification.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high — roughly a quarter of net revenue derives from interest income on customer balances; falling global rates are a structural headwind (retained float yield already above a normalized ~1.5% baseline) partially offset by continued strong balance growth (+31% YoY in Q1 FY27).
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High — Wise operates in dozens of currencies; reporting now in USD (switched from GBP with FY2026 results) increases the visibility of translation effects, and constant-currency growth rates can differ meaningfully from reported growth.
key_input_costs: Compliance, financial-crime, and servicing staff (now a structurally larger, permanent cost base — Servicing + G&A roughly 30-31% of net revenue)
Payment network/banking partner fees and FX liquidity costs
Marketing and brand-building spend (recently increased materially)
Legal/litigation defense costs tied to the new US securities class actions and ongoing Belgian criminal proceedings
macro_factors.regulatory_environment: Increasingly strict globally but trending toward transparency requirements that could favor Wise's disclosed-fee model over opaque bank FX spreads over time; near-term compliance costs remain structurally elevated given the breadth of licenses held, and 2026's successive shocks — the OCC's charter denial, the Belgian criminal AML investigation and subsequent National Bank of Belgium public remedial order (the first under Belgium's new 'name-and-shame' regime), the 2025 US multi-state Consent Order, and the September 2026 US securities class actions — are concrete reminders that Wise's AML/CFT program is currently viewed by multiple regulators and now plaintiffs' counsel — US federal, US state, and Belgian/EU — as below the standard expected for an institution of its scale, despite years of stated investment in compliance.

recent_developments.event: Wise is scheduled to release its Q2 FY27 trading update (quarter ended 30 September 2026) after the US market close, with a conference call the same day; H1 FY27 results and a Goldman Sachs conference presentation are also scheduled for later in the autumn. Not yet reported as of this analysis date (2026-10-06).

Wise's AGM: shareholders passed all eight resolutions by strong majorities, including re-election of directors, auditor matters, and — notably amid the ongoing AML/litigation overhang — authorization for the company to continue repurchasing its own shares (99.98% of votes cast in favor, ~2.10bn votes for vs. 343,312 against; ~74.89% of issued share capital voted).

Multiple US plaintiffs' firms (Kaplan Fox & Kilsheimer, Faruqi & Faruqi, Glancy Prongay & Murray, Levi & Korsinsky) announced/filed federal securities class actions against Wise Group plc on behalf of purchasers of WSE/WISE securities during the class period 11 May 2026-23 July 2026, alleging materially false or misleading statements about AML/CTF controls and US charter risk that were later revealed by the 1 June 2026 Belgian probe disclosure and the 23-24 July 2026 OCC charter denial. Lead-plaintiff deadline was 29 September 2026. No consolidation ruling, motion-to-dismiss outcome, or damages estimate has been disclosed as of early October 2026.

The National Bank of Belgium publicly issued a remedial order against Wise Europe SA — the first company identified under Belgium's new AML enforcement 'name-and-shame' disclosure policy — citing serious deficiencies in customer due diligence (identification/verification of customers and beneficial owners), intra-group information sharing for AML/CTF purposes, ongoing monitoring of business relationships, and examination of unusual activity, and requiring Wise Europe to achieve full compliance by 31 January 2027. The order imposed no monetary fine; it is a supervisory/reputational measure, separate from and not dispositive of the ongoing Brussels Public Prosecutor's criminal investigation, which remains unresolved.

Wise's up-to-£405m (~$540m) share buyback program, executed by Goldman Sachs International across Nasdaq, LSE and other venues (running through 31 March 2027), has been executing steadily: e.g., 800,000 Class A shares on Nasdaq plus 914,573 on the LSE in the week of 7-11 September 2026, and a further 644,479 on Nasdaq plus 849,521 on the LSE in the week of 21-25 September 2026 (~1.49m shares that week alone); ~60% of repurchased shares are held in treasury and ~40% directed to the Employee Share Trust to offset stock-comp dilution.

OCC formally denied Wise's application (filed June 2025) for a national trust bank charter (proposed 'Wise National Trust', Austin, TX; Corporate Decision #1381, letter dated 21 July, communicated 23-24 July), citing insufficient AML/CFT program maturity, organizers/management lacking adequate AML/CFT and fiduciary experience, and Wise US's ongoing noncompliance record tied to the July 2025 multi-state Consent Order. WSE shares fell ~6-9% to ~$11.33 and LSE-listed shares fell as much as 10-11% intraday before partially recovering. Same-day, Wise announced it will submit a new charter application under a GENIUS Act stablecoin/payments framework; independent commentary notes 8 of 11 resolved OCC fintech trust-charter applications since 2020 were approved, making Wise the outlier denial.

Q1 FY27 results (quarter ended 30 June 2026): net revenue $714.0m (+25% YoY, 24% constant currency), cross-border volume $69.3bn (+26%), active customers 11.86m (+21%, business customers 608k +28%), customer holdings $41.2bn (+31%), assets under custody $10.2bn (+55%), take rate 0.50% (-2bps YoY), 77% instant transfers (+7pp). FY27 guidance reiterated: net revenue growth around the middle of the 15-20% medium-term range (constant currency); income-before-tax margin around the top of the 20-25% range.

FY2026 full-year results (first reported in USD under US GAAP): net revenue $2,502.8m (+19% YoY), 18.9m active customers in the year (+21%), cross-border volume $243.5bn (+31% YoY), cross-border take rate 0.52% (down from 0.58% in FY2025 and 0.67% in FY2024), customer holdings $39.0bn (+40% YoY), operating income $590.7m (down from $728.2m in FY2025 due to a heavy investment year), income before tax $660.4m, net income $498.7m, diluted EPS 48.43c. Interest income on customer balances $806.1m gross (+6% YoY). Shares rose roughly 8% on the day.

American Banker/Bureau of Investigative Journalism reported (1 June 2026) that Belgian prosecutors have since 2025 been investigating Wise Europe SA for suspected AML/CFT failures tied to more than EUR500m in suspicious cross-border transactions surfaced via hundreds of criminal files referred from 30+ countries; prosecutors were said to be finalizing a direct summons to Belgian criminal court, with findings also expected to be shared with the National Bank of Belgium. WSE shares fell a cumulative 16.05% over 1-3 June 2026. That NBB referral materialized as a public remedial order on 25 August 2026 (see above); the underlying criminal prosecution itself remains unresolved as of early October 2026, with no charges yet confirmed filed.

Wise completed its US stock market debut, trading on Nasdaq under ticker WSE as its new primary listing, while retaining a secondary listing on the London Stock Exchange (LSE: WISE, quoted in GBp). Reorganization completed May 8, 2026 under new Jersey holding company Wise Group plc (Wise plc renamed Wise Limited, becoming a subsidiary).

WSE traded around $11.44-$11.56 (52-week range ~$10.36-$17.47; market cap ~$13.9bn); the LSE line (WISE.L) traded around 854.8p (52-week range 754.0p-1,101.5p; market cap ~£8.4bn). Sell-side coverage is 'Moderate Buy'/net constructive but has cooled somewhat since the summer: per MarketBeat (early October 2026, ~10 brokerages) 5 Buy, 2 Strong Buy, 3 Hold, average 12-month target ~$16.52; a separate 13-analyst compilation puts the average target at ~$16.94 (implying ~45% upside from spot). JPMorgan remains Overweight (PT $17.30, trimmed from $17.50); Morgan Stanley remains at Equalweight ($16.10 PT, 'mature payments company' framing); Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage with a Buy rating in this period.

Shareholders approved the US primary listing move and a ten-year extension of CEO Kristo Käärmann's Class B supervoting shares (originally scheduled to sunset in 2026, now to 2036), despite public opposition from co-founder Taavet Hinrikus over governance/entrenchment concerns. Käärmann holds ~18% economic interest but retains nearly 50% voting control.

US state regulators (California, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas, Massachusetts, Order No. 2025-013, plus a separate California DFPI order) issued a public Multi-State Consent Order against Wise US, following a 2024 multi-state examination that identified AML/BSA program deficiencies and imposing a $4.2m fine plus a multi-year independent third-party validation, SAR lookback exercise, and quarterly reporting requirement running through July 2027; this Order was subsequently cited directly by the OCC as a central reason for denying Wise's trust bank charter application a year later.

Continued build-out of Wise Platform bank partnerships, including Standard Chartered (SC Remit cross-border remittance service across Asia/Middle East), Morgan Stanley (first investment bank on Wise Platform, corporate cross-border settlement), plus Nubank, UniCredit, Itaú, Monzo, Ramp, and Brex.

Guidance has not been formally revised following the OCC charter denial, the Belgian AML probe/NBB remedial order, or the September 2026 securities class actions; the Q2 FY27 trading update (15 October 2026) is the next scheduled checkpoint.

Servicing + G&A opex (~30-31% of net revenue) now looks like a structural post-remediation cost level rather than a transient spike.

77% in Q1 FY27, up 7 percentage points YoY, driven by additional direct payment-rail integrations.

items.period: No confirmed date as of October 2026; realistic refile not before H2 2027, approval (if any) not before H2 2028

items.notes: Original application was denied by the OCC on AML/CFT-adequacy and management/board-competence grounds. Wise has stated it will submit a new application aligned to the US GENIUS Act stablecoin framework, but has given no confirmed timeline as of the Q1 FY27 update or subsequently; the outstanding Consent Order's independent validation and SAR lookback obligations (through July 2027) are likely to gate credible refiling.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Kristo Käärmann highlighted that nearly 12 million customers moved $69.3bn in Q1 FY27 at an average fee of just 50bps — 'the lowest it has ever been on Wise' — with 77% of transfers delivered instantly and customer holdings up 31% to $41.2bn, and cited the recent Latin America product expansion (Chile) as evidence of continued geographic build-out. On the Belgian AML investigation and subsequent National Bank of Belgium remedial order, Wise has said it is cooperating with Belgian authorities and is implementing a remediation plan to meet the 31 January 2027 compliance deadline, without providing further detail on potential financial exposure from the separate criminal proceedings. Following the 23-24 July 2026 OCC charter denial, management stated the decision 'does not affect Wise's normal operations, in the U.S. and elsewhere,' pointed to its existing 48-state money transmitter license footprint and 80+ global licenses as continuity of service, and committed to submit a new charter application under a GENIUS Act framework. Management has not issued specific public commentary addressing the September 2026 US securities class actions beyond standard litigation disclosure; no reserve has been disclosed. Management continues to frame FY2026 as a peak reinvestment year intended to widen the infrastructure moat and support Wise Platform scaling, with FY2027 margins expected to remain near the top of the 20-25% income-before-tax range.

bull_case: Massive, underpenetrated total addressable market: cross-border payments remain dominated by expensive bank/correspondent-banking rails; Wise holds only a low single-digit share of the multi-trillion-dollar opportunity, leaving a long runway for volume-driven growth

Widening infrastructure moat independent of the US charter/regulatory noise: continued direct integrations into domestic payment systems (Pix, Zengin, and others) drive both faster settlement (77% instant) and structurally lower unit costs that competitors without a decade-plus infrastructure investment cannot easily replicate

Wise Platform optionality: partnerships with global banks (Standard Chartered, Morgan Stanley, UniCredit, Nubank) represent a call option on a much larger B2B2C distribution channel that could materially accelerate volume if scaling continues

Profitable growth with reinvestment discipline and continued capital return: even amid the regulatory/legal overhang, FY2026 delivered a ~26% income-before-tax margin (beating guidance), FY2027 guidance targets the top of a 20-25% margin range, and the company has kept executing its largest-ever buyback (up to £405m/~$540m) through Q3 2026 — reaffirmed by 99.98% shareholder support for buyback authority at the 24 September 2026 AGM — evidencing balance-sheet and cash-generation confidence

Belgian administrative resolution less punitive than feared: the 25 August 2026 National Bank of Belgium order against Wise Europe SA carried no fine, only a reputational measure and a remediation deadline (31 January 2027), suggesting the administrative/supervisory track of the Belgium matter — as distinct from the separate ongoing criminal investigation — may resolve without a direct financial hit

Nasdaq listing as a re-rating catalyst: primary US listing raises visibility with a broader, growth-oriented investor base, potentially narrowing any valuation gap versus US-listed fintech/payments peers and improving access to the largest capital market

Diversifying, stickier revenue base: rapid growth in card/account revenue (+38% YoY in Q1 FY27) and customer holdings (+31% YoY, including 55% growth in Wise Assets AUC) reduces reliance on pure transaction fees and increases customer lifetime value; non-cross-border revenue now over half of total net revenue

Sell-side sentiment remains net constructive: despite a string of negative regulatory/legal headlines, consensus rating is still 'Moderate Buy'/'Buy' (roughly 7 of 10-13 analysts at Buy/Strong Buy as of early October 2026) with average price targets ($16.52-$16.94) implying substantial upside from the ~$11.40s spot price
bear_case: Structural take-rate compression: the strategy of continuously cutting fees to drive volume means revenue growth is perpetually a race between volume growth and price decline; FY2026 take rate of 0.52% (down from 0.67% in FY2024) and further press reports of a ~46bps FY27 target intensify this treadmill

Rate-cut headwind to interest income: roughly a quarter of net revenue comes from interest on customer balances, with FY2026 retained float yield (~2.22%) already well above a more normalized ~1.5% assumption; a global easing cycle is a direct, largely uncontrollable drag on this revenue stream even as balances grow

Systemic, not isolated, AML/compliance failures now compounding into legal liability: US multi-state regulators (2025), the OCC (2026), and Belgian authorities — both prosecutors and, as of August 2026, the National Bank of Belgium via a public remedial order — have each independently identified the same category of deficiency (inadequate customer/transaction due diligence and monitoring) at Wise entities within about fourteen months, and this pattern is now the explicit basis of US securities class actions (Kaplan Fox, Faruqi, Glancy, Levi & Korsinsky) filed in September 2026 covering the 11 May-23 July 2026 period — converting a reputational/regulatory risk into a quantifiable (if not yet quantified) litigation exposure

Belgium's criminal track remains the single largest unresolved tail risk: unlike the no-fine NBB administrative order, the Brussels Public Prosecutor's criminal investigation into Wise Europe SA (EUR500m+ of suspicious flows, summons to criminal court reportedly being finalized since mid-2026) remains open as of October 2026 with no charges yet confirmed, no provision booked, and minimal disclosure — a potential licence-level risk to the EU entity generating ~27% of group net revenue

Unquantified securities litigation exposure: no damages estimate, reserve, or insurance-coverage disclosure has been made public; based on the ~16% and ~6% share-price declines cited in the complaints against a ~$13-14bn market cap at the time, plausible exposure (even using typical securities-fraud settlement benchmarks of low-single-digit percent of market cap) could run into the tens to potentially $100m+ range if claims are not dismissed — a cost not currently reflected in consensus estimates

Stablecoin/crypto-rail disruption risk: regulated, GENIUS Act-aligned stablecoin infrastructure (e.g., Tether/Anchorage's USAT) is already live in the US, while Wise's own attempt to secure comparable bank-grade rails was rejected on AML grounds, with no confirmed GENIUS Act refiling date as of October 2026 and the multi-state Consent Order's remediation tail (through July 2027) likely delaying any refile until H2 2027 at the earliest

Governance overhang: CEO Kristo Käärmann's extended Class B supervoting shares (renewed for a further decade to 2036 in the contentious 2025 vote, opposed by co-founder Hinrikus) concentrate control disproportionate to economic ownership — a persistent governance risk factor for institutional investors, and one the OCC's letter arguably touches on in questioning organizer/management/board experience and accountability

Permanent margin reset, not temporary investment: FY2026 operating income fell materially (to $590.7m from $728.2m) as the company stepped up technology, marketing, headcount, and compliance remediation spend; Servicing + G&A near 30-31% of net revenue looks like a new structural cost floor rather than a peak-year anomaly, and that spend now must also absorb ongoing legal defense costs across multiple fronts

Wise Platform slower than hoped: large bank partnerships take years to scale and are won through competitive RFPs; if flagship partnerships (Standard Chartered, Morgan Stanley, etc.) fail to reach meaningful volume, the B2B2C growth thesis weakens
valuation_context: Since the 4 August 2026 analysis, the regulatory/legal narrative has both resolved partially and expanded: on 25 August 2026 the National Bank of Belgium issued a public (no-fine) remedial order against Wise Europe SA requiring AML/CTF remediation by 31 January 2027 — less punitive than many feared, but the separate Brussels criminal prosecution remains unresolved — while September 2026 brought newly filed US securities class actions (Kaplan Fox, Faruqi, Glancy, Levi & Korsinsky; class period 11 May-23 July 2026; lead-plaintiff deadline 29 September 2026) alleging Wise understated AML/charter risk around its Nasdaq listing, with no damages estimate yet disclosed. Against that, the 24 September 2026 AGM passed all resolutions (including buyback authority) with 99.98% support, and the up-to-£405m buyback has continued executing steadily through September (~1.49m shares in the week of 21-25 September alone). As of 2-4 October 2026, WSE traded around $11.44-$11.56 (market cap ~$13.9bn; 52-week range ~$10.36-$17.47) and the LSE line (WISE.L) traded around 854.8p (market cap ~£8.4bn; 52-week range 754.0p-1,101.5p) — both still well below pre-Belgium-news (June 2026) and pre-OCC-denial (late July 2026) levels, and little changed from the ~$12.13/WSE level seen in early August. Sell-side sentiment remains net constructive but has moderated: as of early October 2026, roughly 7 of 10-13 covering analysts rate the stock Buy/Strong Buy (vs. 2-3 Hold), with average 12-month price targets of $16.52-$16.94 (JPMorgan Overweight, $17.30 PT; Morgan Stanley Equalweight, $16.10 PT, 'mature payments company' framing; Canaccord Genuity initiated Buy in this period) — implying ~45% upside from spot if achieved, though the gap between consensus targets and the depressed spot price also reflects the market pricing in a real probability of further adverse news from the unresolved Belgian criminal case and the new, as-yet-unquantified US securities litigation. The next catalyst is the Q2 FY27 trading update scheduled for 15 October 2026 (quarter ended 30 September 2026), the first results print since the class actions were filed. Overall, the market continues to price Wise as a high-growth fintech/payments infrastructure story carrying a now well-established, multi-front regulatory and legal risk premium — reflecting mid-to-high-teens revenue growth and a mid-20s% income-before-tax margin, but discounted for an unresolved Belgian criminal investigation, an unquantified but plausible US securities-litigation liability, and a stalled US bank-charter/stablecoin path — rather than being valued as a conventional mature payments processor.
